title: Praising Others About Your Strengths
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece introduces what it calls 'Exceptional Endorsement' -- the outsized impact of praise from a respected leader when it lands on the very strength that leader is themselves known for. The author argues most leaders are biased in the opposite direction, being most critical of others on the qualities that stand out about them personally, and proposes deliberately flipping that reflex into recognition instead. The piece closes by framing this as an intentional, learnable practice that shapes how people see themselves.
points: Praise carries more weight when it comes from someone respected for the very strength being praised -- the article calls this Exceptional Endorsement.
Most leaders default to being most critical of others on the qualities that define their own signature strengths, not most generous.
Deliberately flipping that critical reflex into praise is described as intentional practice used by the best leaders.
The payoff is described as shaping how people see themselves, not just how they feel in the moment.
quotes: Those who are respected, trusted, and admired naturally have a greater impact with their praise.
When a respected leader offers specific praise that reflects one of their own signature strengths, people take notice. The praise lands as a genuine endorsement of who they are and what they do.
Because praise from someone who shares the same strength carries a different kind of authority — a higher standard.
The irony is that most leaders are biased the other way. They are most critical of others on the very qualities that stand out about them.
Leaders who set aside their critical reflex and instead recognize their own strengths in others discover something powerful: they can shape how people see themselves.
